name: West Route
approach: Drive to the Berry Patch or Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (Chambers Lake area) off Forest Road 21/2150 on the west side of the Goat Rocks: turn east onto FR 21, continue about 13 miles, turn at the Snowgrass Trail/Chambers Lake sign onto FR 2150, then follow signs to the Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (elev. ~4,650 ft). Hike Trail #96 (Snowgrass) roughly 4 miles and ~2,000 ft of gain along Goat Creek toward Snowgrass Flats, a large subalpine meadow that is closed to camping (use the established sites below it); from there reach the PCT (via Trail #96 or the cutoff Trail #97) and follow it southbound about 2 miles to Cispus Basin, which has an established camp in the trees just above the PCT's Cispus River crossing. Climb to the saddle at the basin's northeast end, then scramble east across the Goat Ledges/Goat Ribs traverse toward Gilbert Peak (often combined with Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak in one traverse day).
descent: Reverse the Goat Ledges/Goat Ribs traverse and white-aggregate-band route back to camp below Snowgrass Flats, then hike out Trail #96.

bivy.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
bivy.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
bivy.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
bivy.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. Camping within Snowgrass Flat itself is prohibited, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

bivy.name: Chambers Lake Campground
bivy.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.
bivy.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
bivy.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served

itinerary: Commonly done as a multi-summit traverse from a camp below Snowgrass Flats: Day 1, hike in to Lower Snowgrass or the timber sites below the flat; Day 2, traverse to and climb Old Snowy Mountain, Ives Peak, and Gilbert Peak in a single long day (reported round-trip totals of ~22 miles and ~7,500 ft cumulative gain/loss for the full multi-peak traverse) before returning to camp; Day 3, hike out.

name: Southwest Route
approach: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Rainy Pass (4,880 ft) near milepost 158, about 35 miles west of Winthrop or 51 miles east of Marblemount. Park at the Rainy Pass North (PCT) trailhead. Hike north on the Pacific Crest Trail through forest and switchbacks to Cutthroat Pass (~6,800 ft), continue past Granite Pass (~6.25 miles in, where snowfields can linger into August) and along a cliff-cut trail toward Methow Pass. About a mile before Methow Pass, a small, unsigned spur trail switchbacks up to Lower and then Upper Snowy Lake (~6,700–7,000 ft) — roughly 10–11 miles and 2,700 ft of gain one-way from the trailhead. Good campsites sit in the meadow near the lakes.
descent: Reverse the route: a short rappel off the summit block, then downclimb the scree/talus gully back to Snowy Lakes camp and out the PCT.
itinerary: Day 1: Drive to the Rainy Pass trailhead, hike ~10–11 miles via the PCT over Cutthroat and Granite Passes to Snowy Lakes, make camp. Day 2: Alpine start from camp, scramble scree/talus to the summit ridge, negotiate the short 5th-class summit block, rappel/downclimb, return to camp, then hike out. Strong parties sometimes complete the whole outing car-to-car in one long day.

name: West Ridge
approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft, Wenatchee River Ranger District), follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north, entering the Glacier Peak Wilderness at 2.6 miles, to Spider Meadow (about 4.5-5 miles from the trailhead). Continue past Spider Meadow on the climbers' path, staying right of the tumbling creek to scramble up slabs past waterfalls, then continue up grass, talus, and heather slopes trending northeast into upper Phelps Basin. A commonly used bivy sits around 5,700-5,800 ft near treeline with stream access (the basin above 6,000 ft often has only snow-patch camping). In upper Phelps Basin the trail fades; in late July staying climbers-left to about 5,800 ft, then turning right toward the main drainage under Dumbell, worked well, and a bootpath beside that gully shows in early September. The access road is rocky, so bring some clearance.
descent: Reverse the ascent: downclimb the West Ridge talus to the notch/col, then reverse the exposed connecting ledge along Dumbell's east face and the scree/talus gully back into upper Phelps Basin, retracing the approach to Spider Meadow and the trailhead.
itinerary: Most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip: Day 1, hike in roughly 5 miles from the Phelps Creek Trailhead to a camp in upper Phelps Basin (~5,700-5,800 ft); Day 2, climb Dumbell and/or Greenwood via the connecting col and ledge (round trips from camp have taken roughly 8-11 hours) and return to camp; Day 3, hike out. Some strong parties have done both summits car-to-car in a single very long day (one recorded example: ~18 miles round trip with about 5,800 ft of cumulative gain, ~10 hours 45 minutes, covering both Dumbell and Greenwood).

name: Gunnshy Peak Standard Route (Barclay Lake Approach)
approach: From Monroe, drive east on US-2 to the town of Baring. Near milepost 41-42, across from a convenience store, turn left (north) onto 635th Place NE. Cross the railroad tracks and continue about 0.3 mile to a junction; keep left on 635th Place NE for another 0.1 mile, where the road becomes Forest Road 6024 (Barclay Creek Road). Continue roughly 3.9-4.3 miles of gravel forest road (watch for potholes and rough patches; AWD/4x4 recommended after wet weather) to the Barclay Lake Trailhead (vault toilet on site, parking for roughly 20 vehicles, Northwest Forest Pass required). From a spur road near the trailhead, follow the spur toward an old fire pit, where a faint, mostly-unmarked climber's path heads east into the forest and begins the ascent proper. Partway up the steep forested section the path can seem to stop at a gully; the continuing bootpath leaves to the climber's left, and the gully itself goes only at greater difficulty.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — back through the basin/saddle area, across the waterfall gully, and down the steep forested headwall to the Barclay Creek crossing and trailhead spur.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

itinerary: Single-day round trip from the Barclay Lake Trailhead: drive to trailhead, hike the spur road and climber's path via Barclay Creek crossing and the forested headwall, cross the waterfall gully, work along the ridge past the Tailgunner/Wing saddle and Point 5,760+ (via Gunn Lake basin in summer/fall or the open-slope bypass in winter/spring), scramble the summit block, then retrace the entire route back to the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Ridge Junction (Gunn-Barclay Divide, above waterfall gully)

name: Gunrunner
approach: Middle Peak shares the same approach as South Peak: from Downey Creek Trailhead, follow the southern Ptarmigan Traverse cross-country route (Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake, Bachelor Creek) to reach the range's ridge. Expect a multi-day glaciated approach with route-finding and bushwhacking, not a drive-up or short-trail access.
descent: Rappel the south side of each summit during the traverse; from South Peak, rappel to the Blue Glacier, finishing with a free-hanging rappel over the moat.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road has been closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. On top of that, the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) closes the Downey Creek Trailhead, the Downey Creek Trail and the Bachelor Creek Trail from August 15 through December 31, 2026, unless rescinded sooner. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

itinerary: Day 1: Downey Creek Trailhead to Bachelor Flats camp (6 miles, 3,100 ft gain). Day 2: Bachelor Flats to Dome-Chickamin Col base camp (3.2 miles, 2,600 ft gain). Day 3: Climb Gunrunner traverse of four peaks (6-8 hours climbing time, 1,500 ft gain). Day 4: Descend to base camp, then return to Bachelor Flats (5-6 hours). Day 5: Return to trailhead (6 miles, 4,500 ft loss).

name: Improbable Traverse
approach: From Alpental Ski Area parking lot (3,120 ft), reach the talus cone below the west face by a line that stays off the private Alpental Community Club roads; the 'Strasse' roads off the access road are closed to walking and driving, and no established path exists. Approach time ~30 minutes to 1 hour from parking. In early August a public roadside pullout just past the private Strasse entrance serves as parking; keep to the left side of the talus where the rock is less loose.
descent: Traverse north over subsummits with climbers' trail; descent varies seasonally. Alternative: rappel from tree anchors on east side of summit to bypass exposed terrain and avoid reverse-traversing dangerous sections. Some descend via Southeast Couloir toward Cave Ridge and Snow Lake trail.

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

itinerary: Single-day car-to-car outing from Seattle. Leave the city by 4:30-5:00 am, park at Alpental, be scrambling the talus cone by first light, aim to be starting the roped climbing within an hour of leaving the car. Expect roughly 4-5 hours on the face, then 1.5-2 hours over the three summits and down the Cave Ridge trail. Published trip reports range from about 8 hours for a fast, competent pair to 14+ hours for a party that pitches everything out - one well-known report started at 10:30 am and exited at 1 am. There is no reason to camp; if you want a relaxed day, camp at a Snoqualmie Pass area campground the night before rather than on the mountain.

name: Southeast Gully
approach: Start from the Pacific Crest Trail North (Snoqualmie Pass North) trailhead, just off I-90 exit 52. Follow the old Commonwealth Basin trail north for approximately 1.4 miles, until Guye Peak lies directly west or northwest of you. From there head straight upslope - the gully initiates directly above. The approach is on maintained trail or, in winter, on whatever bootpack exists, and is short by Cascade standards; the difficulty is judging the snow on the slope between the trail and the base of the gully, which is itself avalanche terrain on a loaded day.
descent: Walk off from the summit ridge - either west over the Guye / Cave Ridge saddle to the Alpental parking area, or back east down the Commonwealth trail.

Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.

itinerary: A short winter day. From the PCT North trailhead, hike about 1.4 miles up the old Commonwealth Basin trail until the peak is directly west-northwest, then break uphill to the base of the gully. Climb 1,400 ft of snow that steepens from 45 to about 70 degrees, top out on the ridge between the true and false summits, and walk off east down Commonwealth or west over Cave Ridge. Start before dawn so the gully is still frozen: the sun-exposed half of the route softens quickly and the entire line becomes a wet-slide problem once it warms. There is nothing here that justifies an overnight.
