itinerary: Typically climbed as a quick add-on from an established Klawatti/icecap camp (see the Southeast Face route's 3-day traverse itinerary): approach and camp on Day 1-2, then climb the SW Buttress in 1-2 hours on a summit day alongside or instead of the south face.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)

name: Northeast Ridge
approach: From the North Fork Skykomish / Quartz Creek Trailhead at the end of FR 63 (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF, Skykomish Ranger District, via Beckler Road FR 65), follow the Quartz Creek Trail about 4 miles, gaining roughly 1,450 ft, to Curry Gap (~4,000 ft) at the Bald Eagle Mountain Trail junction. From Curry Gap head west/southwest along an up-and-down ridge toward Kyes, leaving the ridge where feasible to cross the Pride Glacier west-northwest toward the cliffs below Monte Cristo Peak, reaching the northeast base of Kyes around 6,000 ft.
descent: Reverse the ridge/glacier line back to Curry Gap and the Quartz Creek Trail.
itinerary: Long single push from the North Fork Sauk trailhead, or split over two days with a camp near Curry Gap or on the ridge. Mike Heath's 1968 first-ascent account describes the outing from the road's end as taking about 4-5 hours, though this reflects a fast/direct climb rather than a typical modern car-to-car day given the approach length.

name: Northern Aspect
approach: Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount (paved for roughly the first third, then gravel, narrow and steep near the end) 23.1 miles to the Cascade Pass Trailhead (road-end elevation about 3,660 ft). Hike the Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles / 1,700 ft gain to Cascade Pass, then continue cross-country/on climbers' path south on the Ptarmigan Traverse: ascend the Cache Glacier to Cache Col (~6,900 ft), descend to Kool-Aid Lake (~6,100 ft), cross the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier, climb to the Spider-Formidable col (~7,300 ft), and descend to Yang Yang Lakes (~5,800 ft), which serves as the standard base camp below Le Conte's north side. This approach alone is a full day of glacier travel with sustained elevation gain and loss.
descent: Reverse the summit ledges and east-slope talus/snow back to Yang Yang Lakes camp, then retrace the Ptarmigan Traverse approach back over the Middle Cascade Glacier, Kool-Aid Lake, and Cache Col/Cache Glacier to Cascade Pass and out the trail to the trailhead.

bivy.name: Le Conte Pass
bivy.notes: The pass sits on the shoulder above the lakes in the basin below Le Conte Mountain, and it is the direct base for Le Conte itself, which is climbed by working up its east slope on talus and blocky rock by the line of least resistance rather than by any single defined route. It is also where parties running late stop instead of dropping into and re-climbing out of the steep basin below, which is the trade that decides most itineraries on this stretch: better position and worse water, against reliable water and a thousand feet of extra work. From the pass the next day crosses the Le Conte Glacier, which is the most broken ice on this part of the crest and has turned parties around outright, so this is a camp to leave early and roped. Published elevations for the pass vary, so treat the figure as approximate.
bivy.water: Small tarns at the pass hold water through midsummer and are the practical source, but they are snowmelt pools with tiny catchments and they can be gone or foul by September. Late in the season this is a dry camp and the lakes below are the honest answer.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Keep camps back from the tarns, camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather, and pack out human waste. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: Heather and gravel benches around the pass and its tarns, enough for two or three parties spread out. Unimproved, no toilet.

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: Reached by crossing Spider-Formidable Col and descending snow and scree. The standard camp for Le Conte, which is climbed from here in a day.
bivy.water: The lakes and a stream
bivy.permit: No permit required (Glacier Peak Wilderness)
bivy.capacity: Many established sites, the best at the south end of the south lake

bivy.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
bivy.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
bivy.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
bivy.permit: This is the last ground on the park side, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

bivy.name: Spider-Formidable Col
bivy.notes: The working base camp for both Spider Mountain and Mount Formidable, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
bivy.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

itinerary: Typical 2-3 day plan: Day 1 — drive to Cascade Pass Trailhead, hike to Cascade Pass and over Cache Col/Cache Glacier, descend to Kool-Aid Lake, cross Middle Cascade Glacier to Yang Yang Lakes camp (a long day, ~9,000+ ft cumulative gain over ~13 miles). Day 2 — climb Le Conte Mountain round-trip from camp via the east-slope/ledge route. Day 3 — reverse the approach back to the trailhead.

name: Goatshead Spire
approach: Identical to the Lemah Glacier approach, which is the only documented way into this cirque. From I-90 exit 80 (Roslyn / Salmon la Sac) go north on Bullfrog Road 2.8 miles through two roundabouts, continue on WA-903 past Cle Elum Lake (about 16.8 miles total from the freeway), turn west on FR-46 and follow it roughly 4.7-5 miles, then turn right on FR-4616 for 1-1.5 miles to the Pete Lake trailhead at about 2,800 ft (47.4350, -121.1855). Hike Cooper River / Pete Lake Trail 1323 about 4.4 flat miles to Pete Lake (2,979 ft), continue about 1.3 miles to a junction and stay right without crossing the creek, then 0.8 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn left (south) on the PCT for about 0.8 miles to Lemah Creek at roughly 3,200 ft; the PCT bridge over South Lemah Creek washed out in the winter of 2007/08 and parties still cross on a log about 20 yards downstream. Leave the trail at the creekside campsite and follow an old flagged climbers' path on the north side of Lemah Creek, with moderate alder and vine-maple bushwhacking, gaining about 400 ft in half a mile to the lower grassy meadow near 3,600 ft. Continue up dry stream beds toward the large snow finger and into the cirque below Lemah Two's east side; the towers on the east spur are directly above.
descent: Unpublished. Assume rappelling the line of ascent from gear you place or from natural anchors, then reverse the snow and creek approach.

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
bivy.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

itinerary: Realistically a three-day trip. Day 1: drive to Pete Lake trailhead and hike 7-8 miles of easy trail to the PCT campsite by Lemah Creek at about 3,200 ft, or camp at Pete Lake. Day 2: leave camp before first light, follow the climbers' path and snow finger into the east-side cirque, climb the spire, and return to camp. Day 3: hike out. A fit party has done the neighbouring standard route car-to-car in 11 hours 26 minutes, but that is a snow scramble with a known line; an obscure rock tower with no known line deserves the extra day.

name: Southeast Ridge (from Lichtenwasser Lake)
approach: Summer: drive US 2 to the Smith Brook Road / FR 6700 turnoff 3.5 miles east of Stevens Pass and follow the unpaved road up toward the Smithbrook Trailhead. Park at or near the first major switchback and find the Lichtenwasser Lake fishing trail, which leads roughly southeast then south through forest to the lake at 4,708 ft (47.7924, -121.0768). From the south end of the lake leave any semblance of path and climb southwest up open and lightly wooded slopes to the broad 5,640-foot saddle on the mountain's southeast ridge; turn right (northwest) and follow the ridge to the summit. Winter: FR 6700 is unplowed, so park on the shoulder of US 2 at or just before the Smith Brook Road turnoff, around mileposts 68.7-68.9 and 4 miles east of Stevens Pass, and skin or snowshoe 2 to 2.6 miles up the snow-covered road — it is usually well packed by other parties. Leave the road at the first major hairpin (near 3,970 ft), head southwest and then follow a bearing of 177 degrees true to Lichtenwasser Lake, crossing it when frozen, and continue on 248 degrees to the 5,640-foot saddle before finishing up the ridge.
descent: Reverse the southeast ridge to the 5,640 ft saddle and descend northeast to Lichtenwasser Lake and the road; skiers descend the same north-side slopes.
itinerary: Summer: a single easy day, about 7 miles round trip with about 2,100 ft of gain. Brisbine's party made an overnight of it in September, camping at Lichtenwasser Lake and taking in both the true summit and The Lichtenhorn the following day — a pleasant way to do it if you want an unhurried trip. Winter: a full but moderate day tour, about 5.2 to 8 miles and 2,100 to 2,700 ft of gain from US 2, with the road approach taking a good chunk of the time. Start early in winter to have the road walk behind you before the snow softens and to keep your options open on stability.

waypoints.name: Smith Brook Road (FR 6700) — first major switchback, start of the Lichtenwasser Lake approach
Lichtenwasser Lake — camp and the launching point for the 248-degree bearing to the saddle

name: West Face (5.9+ rock route)
approach: Drive US 2 to the Smith Brook Road / FR 6700 turnoff 3.5 miles east of Stevens Pass (31 miles west of Leavenworth) and follow the unpaved road roughly 2.5-3 miles to the Smithbrook Trailhead at about 4,000 ft. Hike Smithbrook Trail #1590 for 0.9 mile to the PCT at Union Gap, turn left (south) onto the PCT #2000 and follow it 1.7 miles over the ridge crest and down toward Lake Valhalla at 4,836 ft — about 3.5 miles and 1,500 ft of gain in total. The west face rises directly above the lake's east shore, roughly 1,000 ft of relief. The 2002 report gives the walk in as about an hour, which implies a fast pace on this trail. Scope the wall from the lake or from the PCT high point on the way in; there is no marked or described start.
descent: Not documented in any available source. Parties presumably walk off by the mountain's easier southwest or northeast slopes.
itinerary: A single day from the Smithbrook trailhead is what the original report implies: roughly an hour in, climb, walk off, and out. Camping at Lake Valhalla — dispersed sites set back from the shore, campfires prohibited — puts you directly under the wall and would suit a party wanting time to scope the line before committing.

waypoints.name: Lake Valhalla — directly beneath the west face; scope the line from here
